title: The Science of Happiness · Episode 2
chapters: Laughter: it's not really about jokes

units.t: The Science of Happiness. Episode two.
In this episode: Friendship and loneliness, Laughter: it's not really about jokes and Meaning and purpose.
Part one. Friendship and loneliness.
Researchers compare the health risks of chronic loneliness to smoking.
Friendship might be the most underrated health habit there is.
Built to belong.
Humans evolved in groups, where being cut off meant danger: fewer people to share food, spot predators or care for you when sick.
In 1995, Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued that the need to belong is a fundamental motivation, like hunger or thirst.
Brain imaging suggests rejection activates some of the regions involved in physical pain, though the overlap is debated.
The health stakes are real.
A 2010 review by Julianne Holt-Lunstad covered 148 studies and over 300,000 people.

Those with stronger social relationships had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival over an average of about seven and a half years, an effect compared with risks like smoking and physical inactivity.
Loneliness is also linked to heart disease, stroke, depression and dementia.
Alone versus lonely.
Being alone isn't the same as being lonely.
Loneliness is the painful feeling that your relationships fall short of your needs, in number or depth.
Social isolation is an objective measure, like living alone.
You can feel lonely in a crowded office, a share house or a marriage.
Young adults report high loneliness, not just older people.
In 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory on an 'epidemic of loneliness and isolation', and Australian surveys suggest a substantial share of adults often feel lonely.
John Cacioppo argued loneliness works like a warning signal that we're socially unsafe.
Lonely people slept less restfully, showed higher stress and inflammation, and read neutral faces as unfriendly, so they withdrew further.
That wariness is a normal response to isolation, not proof that others dislike you.
How friendships form.

Communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated in 2018 that it takes roughly 50 hours together to move from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 hours to become a friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends.
What you do together matters too: joking around, catching up and meaningful conversation built closeness faster than small talk.
Friendship grows from proximity and repetition, seeing the same people regularly at school, work, a club or a sports team.
That's why adult friendships take more effort, and why regular shared activities matter so much.
Time together is the raw ingredient.
Quality and small moments.
Robin Dunbar suggested people can maintain roughly five very close relationships, about 15 good friends and 150 meaningful ones, the last figure known as Dunbar's number.
The figures are rough and debated, but the inner circle matters most for wellbeing.
Lighter contact counts too.
Chicago commuters asked by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder to chat with a stranger on the train enjoyed the ride more than those told to sit quietly, although most had predicted the opposite.
Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn found that on days with more brief chats with 'weak ties', like baristas, classmates and neighbours, people felt happier and more connected.
Reaching out.
People underestimate how much others appreciate being contacted, especially out of the blue.
So message the old friend, invite someone for a coffee or walk, and join something that meets regularly, like a community garden, sporting club, men's shed or choir.
Volunteering is a good way in too.
Show up consistently, since reliability builds trust.
Research on technology is mixed.
Video calls and messages keep relationships alive across distance.
Active use is linked to feeling more connected, while passive scrolling is linked to feeling worse, though not all research agrees.
Ask whether an app leads to real contact or replaces it.
If loneliness feels overwhelming or persistent, talk to a GP or counsellor.
In Australia, Lifeline, 13 11 14, is available 24 hours a day.
The key idea: Belonging is a basic human need, and people with stronger relationships had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival in a large review.
Part two. Laughter: it's not really about jokes.
We think we laugh because something is funny.
One scientist spent years eavesdropping on laughing strangers and found that most laughter has nothing to do with humour at all.
Laughter isn't about jokes.
In the 1990s neuroscientist Robert Provine, of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, took a simple approach.
Rather than showing people comedy in a lab, he and his students hung around shopping centres, campuses and city streets, noting what people had just said when someone laughed.
Across more than a thousand episodes, only around 10 to 20 per cent of laughs followed anything like a joke.
Most came after lines such as 'I'll see you guys later' or 'Are you sure?'
Speakers also laughed more than their listeners.
Laughter, Provine concluded, is less a reaction to comedy than a social signal: a way of saying we are friendly, relaxed and on the same side.
Laughter is for company.
If laughter were just about funny things, you would laugh as much alone as with friends.
You don't.

In diary studies, Provine found people laughed about 30 times more often in social situations than alone, and much of what they laughed at alone came from television or radio, which supply a kind of company.
Laughter is also contagious.

Hearing others laugh makes us more likely to laugh, which is why television producers began adding canned laughter in the 1950s, using a machine nicknamed the 'laff box', invented by sound engineer Charley Douglass.
Most people say they dislike laugh tracks, yet studies have found they can make people laugh more at the same jokes.
Older than words.
Laughter is far older than language.
Chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans make breathy panting sounds when they play-wrestle or are tickled.
Researchers who compared these sounds found a family tree of laughter that matches the apes' evolutionary relationships.
Ape laughter pants in and out with each breath, while human laughter chops a single outward breath into rhythmic 'ha-ha-ha' bursts.
The roots may go deeper.
In the late 1990s neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that rats make high-pitched chirps, too high for human ears, when tickled, and tickled rats chase the researcher's hand for more.
In mammals, laughter seems to have begun as a signal that rough play is only play.
Real and fake.
Neuroscientist Sophie Scott, of University College London, separates spontaneous laughter, which bursts out of us, from volitional laughter, the polite laugh we produce on purpose.
Brain imaging shows partly different areas respond to each, and people can usually tell them apart.
In a 2014 study by Gregory Bryant and Athena Aktipis, sped-up spontaneous laughs began to sound like animal calls, while deliberate ones still sounded human.
That suggests real laughter relies on an older vocal system than speech does.
Deliberate laughter is not dishonest; it is often a kind, useful signal.
Smiles work similarly.
Guillaume Duchenne, a nineteenth century French neurologist, noted that real joy also tightens the muscle around the eye, creating crow's feet.
But many people can fake this, so it is not a foolproof test.
Good company, not medicine.
Social laughter does something useful.
In 2012 a team led by evolutionary psychologist Robin Dunbar found that people who laughed together at comedy videos could tolerate more pain than those who watched dull films.
They linked this to the brain's own opioid-like chemicals.
Shared laughter helps people feel closer, soothes tension and makes tough situations bearable, as anyone in a hard job with dark humour knows.
But claims that laughter cures disease, or that a set number of laughs replaces exercise, go far beyond the evidence.
Contagion can reach extremes.
In 1962 at a girls' school in Kashasha, Tanganyika, now Tanzania, uncontrollable laughing spread to villages and affected roughly a thousand people over months.
No infection or poison was found; it is described as mass psychogenic illness, a physical response spreading through a group under stress.
The key idea: Studies of everyday conversation found most laughter follows ordinary remarks, because it works as a social signal.
Part three. Meaning and purpose.
A happy life and a meaningful life aren't quite the same thing.
Research suggests you need both.
Happiness versus meaning.
A 2013 study by Roy Baumeister and colleagues surveyed about 400 Americans.
Happiness was linked to getting what you want and feeling good in the present.
Meaning was linked to reflecting on past and future, contributing to others and expressing who you are, and it sometimes came with stress and struggle.
Takers were happier; givers found more meaning.
Raising children can lower moment-to-moment happiness while bringing some of the deepest meaning people report.
Frank Martela and Michael Steger proposed in 2016 that meaning has three parts: coherence, your life makes sense, purpose, goals and direction, and significance, your life matters to someone.
A new retiree may keep coherence but lose the purpose work provided.
Frankl and purpose.
Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was deported by the Nazis in 1942 and survived several camps, including Auschwitz.
His wife, parents and brother died in the Holocaust.
In Man's Search for Meaning, 1946, he argued that people can endure almost anything if they find meaning in it, and that we keep the freedom to choose our attitude.
He saw meaning in creating, in love or beauty, and in how we face unavoidable suffering.
His therapy is called logotherapy, from the Greek logos, 'meaning'.
Purpose is also linked to lower risks of heart disease, stroke, dementia and early death, even after accounting for income and education.
A 2019 analysis of about 7,000 Americans over 50 found the lowest purpose scores predicted earlier death.
Cause is uncertain, as healthier people may find purpose easier.
Where meaning comes from.
Research points to a few common sources of meaning.
Close relationships come first for most people.
Contributing matters too, through paid work, volunteering, parenting or caring for someone.
So do growth and mastery, whether in carpentry, coaching or a language.
Many find meaning in something larger: a community, cause, nature, faith or tradition.
It's usually found by doing, and grows from commitments already made.
Ikigai, Japanese for roughly 'reason for being', often refers to everyday sources of purpose, like a hobby, a role in the family or community work, not a grand mission.
The popular four-circle diagram is a Western addition.
Aristotle's eudaimonia, flourishing through living well, is a similar idea.
Meaning at work.
Psychologist Amy Wrzesniewski found people tend to see their work in one of three ways: as a job, done mainly for pay; a career, focused on advancement; or a calling, worthwhile in itself.
Surprisingly, all three views appeared among people doing the same role, such as administrative assistants.
In a study of hospital cleaners, some saw the work as purely cleaning, while others emphasised comforting patients and helping nurses, and found it far more meaningful.
Researchers call this job crafting: reshaping your tasks, relationships or how you think about your work to connect it with what you value.
Finding more meaning.
You don't need a grand mission.
At the end of each day, ask: what did I do that mattered to someone?
Look for ways to use your strengths to help others, even in small ways.
Reflect on your values and check whether your calendar matches them.
Tell your story, too.
Psychologist Dan McAdams found that people who see their lives as stories of growth or redemption, where hard times led to something good, tend to report more meaning and wellbeing.
Meaning can grow from difficulty, not just despite it, a point Frankl made from painful experience.
The key idea: Happiness is feeling good now, while meaning comes from purpose, contribution and a life that makes sense.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Holt-Lunstad's large review find about relationships and survival?
Answer. Stronger ties gave a roughly 50 per cent greater chance of survival.
Question two. What did Provine's street observations find about what people laughed at?
Answer. Most laughs followed ordinary remarks, not jokes.
Question three. How did Baumeister's study separate meaning from happiness?
Answer. Happiness was about getting; meaning was about giving.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
